Closure of STD/ISD 
1642. SHRIMATI AMBIKA SO NI: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the closure of STD/ISD and Internet was step to 
check and control terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir; 
(b) if so, what are the reasons that made the Centre backtrack; 
(c) whether it is a fact that in an unfruitful attempt to control terrorism the 
genuine people of Jammu and Kashmir were deprived of basic 
communication by Centre's earlier decision; and 
90 

[1 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) if so, what is the estimate of the loss in terms of business and finance 
that could have generated by the Communication department due to Centre's 
decision? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY 
(SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) to (d) The STD/ISD service on 
PCO booths in 12 districts of Jammu and Kashmir and Internet service in Jammu 
and Kashmir State were suspended in the month of December, 2001/January, 
2002 in view of security considerations. Government had been keeping a watch 
on the situation and a considered decision was taken in May, 2002 to restore 
these facilities keeping in view the totality of circumstances. 
STD/ISD facility was withdrawn only from private PCOs working 
under franchise scheme. However, STD/ISD facility was available to 
customers on house/office telephones.There was hardly any loss to BSNL due to 
withdrawl of STD/ISD facility. 
The Internet service are pre-paid account services. No separate bills are 
issued to users. The loss on this account cannot be quantified because the calls 
come in the category of local calls.

(c) The details of the steps taken to plug loopholes and contain

(d) Various steps taken by the FCI to weed out corruption are: (a)

officials working in the field do not taken undue advantage of any lacunae, (b)

institution of criminal cases, as warrant ed, (d) Stricter surveillance on high-
loss reporting depots, (e) Surprise checks at the time of loading/unloading of 
the stocks by the Regional, Zonal and Headquarters Squads.

and distribution of foodgrains. Since the Minimum Support Price for 
procurement & Central Issue Prices for distribution are determined by the 
Government, the Government reimburses the differential on account of FCI's 
operational expenses. 
Statement 
The following steps have been taken by the Government and the Food 
Corporation of India to plug loopholes and contain leakages in transportation 
and storage of foodgrains: 
(a) Adoption of 50 Kg. packing in a phased manner to avoid use of 
hooks. 
(b) Installation of electronic lorry weighbridges. 
(c) Administrative measures such as ti ghtening of security at depots, 
intensifying surprise checks, ensuring regular stock verification etc.

(e) Induction of Central Industrial Security Force at vulnerable depots to curb 
theft and pilferage. 
(f) To streamline procedure and documentation for transporency and 
accountability in operations at each level. 
(g) Special squad checking at selected railhead, transhipment and 
destination/despatch centres. 
(h) Identification of vulnerable points. 
(i) Speed up fixation of responsibility and recoveries of the losses 
wherever called for. 
(j) Inspection of depots by Senior Officers and Headquarters, Zonal 
Managers/Senior Regional Manager/District Managers. 
(k) Regular inspection of weighbridges. 
(I) Improvement in size and quality of gunnies.

Recommendations of Prof. Abhijit Sen Committee 
1662. PROF. RAM DEO BHANDA RY: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government have recei ved recommendations of Prof. 
Abhijit Sen Committee set up on Food Management Policy; 
(b) if so, the recommendations made therein; and 
(c) the action taken or proposed to be taken by Government on each of these 
recommendations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI U.V. KRISHNAM 
RAJU): (a) The High Level committee (HLC) to formulate a Long Term 
109 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2002] 
Grain Policy has submitted its final report on 31.7.2002. 
(b) The Committee has made fa r-reaching recommendations with 
regard to the policy in the short as well as long run on:— 
(i) Foodgrains-based welfare schemes; 
(ii) Public Distribution System; 
(iii) Minimum Support Prices and Procurement Policy; 
(iv) Policy on Open Market Sales, Exports and Imports; 
(v) Role of private trade; and 
(vi) FCI 
The details of these recommendations are annexed as statement. (See 
below,) 
(c) These recommendations will be examined by the Government. 
Statement 
Major Long Run and Short Run Recommendations made by the High Level 
Committee on Long Term Grain Policy 
Long Run Recommendations 
(i) Welfare Schemes 
With regard to the welfare schemes, the Committee- has recommended a 
massive foodgrains employment programme, expansion of the existing 
Antyodaya scheme to cover the entire destitute population, Central support for 
moving to a cooked Mid day Meals scheme for all school-going children and 
strengthening programmes for women and children. 
(ii) PDS 
With regard to the Public Distribution System, the Committee has 
recommended a system of Universal PDS with uniform Central Issue Prices 
for rice and wheat for all consumers in all parts of the country. The Committee 
has also recommended that an additional subsidy meant for poor consumers or 
persons in relatively backward regions should be given in cash to States. Other 
recommendations for streamlining the PDS include 
110 

[1 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
the setting up of an independent watchdog body, relaxation of restrictions on 
eligibility to be a licensed fair price shop dealer, effective implementation of the 
PDS (Control) Order, 2001 and greater responsibilities to be given to 
Panchayati Raj Institutions. 
(iii) MSP and Procurement Policy 
With regard to Minimum Supp ort Prices, the Committee has 
recommended that the MSP policy should continue with an immediate 
correction. The Committee has reco mmended that the Commission for 
Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) should go strictly on the basis of C2 cost 
of production (i.e. all costs including the imputed costs of family labour, owned 
capital and rental on land) in more efficient regions. It has also recommended 
that the MSP should have statutory status and the CACP should be made an 
empowered statutory body. 
It has further recommended to take care of the States which impose 
excessive levies on MSP purchase, the Central Government may announce its MSP 
policy by declaring a procurement price inclusive of a uniform 4% allowance, 
which should be the maximum price payable for MSP purchases. At this MSP 
price, the Central Government should underwrite open-ended purchase of FAQ 
grains to assure growers an adequate return on their cost. 
The Committee has also recommended that FCI's operation should focus 
more on Eastern and Central India than in the past. The Committee has further 
recommended that while the Central should continue to take primary 
responsibility for procurement, procurement should also become more 
dispersed. With regard to coarsegrains, the Committee has recommended that 
MSP operations should be decentrali zed to State Governments with full 
financial support from the Centre. 
Another major recommendation of the Committee is that all 
compulsory levy orders on rice millers  under the Essential Commodities Act 
should be removed with immediate effect and be replaced by orders requiring 
mills to custom mill the paddy procured under MSP and give delivery of the 
resultant rice to the Central Pool. 
To ensure improvement in quality, the Committee has recommended that 
Fair Average Quality (FAQ) norms should be adhered to strictly in all purchases 
of grains. In unforeseen circumstances if below FAQ norms 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2002] 
grains are procured, they should not be taken to the Central Pool and should 
be disposed of at commercial terms. 
Along with the correct MSP policy, the Committee has recommended that 
the Central Government should explor e expeditiously with the insurance 
sector the commercial viability of insurance, devised strictly on actuarial 
principles, against shortfalls not only of yield but also of prices from their past 
averages computed on an area basis. Any start-up subsidy required for this 
should be phased out within two years of implementation for all except poor 
and marginal farmers. 
The Committee has also recommended measures for crop 
diversification given the changing dietary patterns. 
(iv) Open market sales, export and imports 
With regard to open market sales, the Committee has recommended that the 
prices should be based on the corresponding Central Issue Prices plus the full cost 
of transport and storage as well as market conditions. 
With regard to export and imports of foodgrains, the Committee has 
recommended that it should be based on the system of variable tariffs and the 
exports should be entirely on private account. 
(v) Role of private trade 
The Committee has recommended that barriers to private trade should be 
eased.The Essential Commodities Act should in normal circumstances apply only 
to situations of natural disasters or  other contingencies. However, it has 
recommended that a new set of orders, on the lines of PDS (Control) Order, 2001 
may be required to apply to those who voluntarily enter activities 
encompassed in public procurement and distribution. 
(vi) FCI 
With regard to the Food Corporation of India, the Committee has 
expressed the opinion that it has performed its role reasonably well and should 
continue to do so. It has recommended that FCI should move into areas where 
reports of distress sale continue to be received and in such areas FCI should open 
procurement centres. It has further recommended that FCI should change the way 
it does business to enable fast commercial oriented decision-making. It has 
recommended that the FCI should develop a work culture of total quality 
management. The Committee has 
112 

[1 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
recommended that the FCI's role should be confined to procurement of major 
cereals for the PDS, i.e. rice and wheat and price support operations in coarse 
cereals should be handled by State agencies. 
The Committee has suggested that the FCI should identify areas of cost 
control by normating of FCI's costs based on the norms recommended by the 
BICP.The Committee has also suggested several measures to cut down the 
storage and transit losses. 
Short Run Recommendations 
For the immediate short run, the Committee has recommended lowering 
of the MSP to average C2 cost, steps to be taken to give statutory status to MSP, 
removal of levy orders on rice millers and strict maintenance of quality 
specifications. Lowering of the C2 cost has been recommended along with a 
compensation package to be given to State Governments for compensating its 
cultivators, estimated at a total of Rs. 3915 crores. 
The Committee has recommended that the State Governments should be free to 
offer this compensation to farmers in any one or combination of the following: 
i) Direct per hectare transfer to farmers 
ii) Subsidising premiums on insurance schemes on crop incomes/ yield 
iii) Specific crop diversification schemes 
iv) Other credit/input linked schemes to offset cost, including electricity 
The other recommendations for the short run, including shifting of the 
FCI's focus to East and Central India and removal of existing bottlenecks in the 
decentralized procurement system. 
The Committee has recommended several stock reduction measures, including 
disposal of old and relaxed quality stocks. It has recommended that the lustre 
lost stocks of wheat should be liquidated by March 31, 2003 and all possible 
steps should be taken to segregate available stocks by age and quality. 
It has further recommended that th e FCI implements the method of 
physical verification within a period of three months, keeping in view the new 
sampling method proposed by the ISI. 
113 
 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2002] 
With regard to exports, the Committee has recommended that steps should 
be taken to prevent leakages into th e domestic market and a review of the 
current export drive should be taken up as and when stocks come down to 35 
million tonnes. 
With regard to the PDS, the Committee has endorsed an immediate shift to 
a unified PDS, which in its view, would bring back many of the poor and 
moderately poor who have been excluded from the BPL category. The unified 
system should be accompanied by a uni form CIP for all consumers at Rs. 
4.50 per kg of wheat and Rs. 6 per kg of rice to be accompanied by a transfer 
of 35 paisa per kg of grain offtake as cash incentive to State Governments, 
conditional on lifting and accounting. This should be till stocks reduce 
sufficiently, after which the CIP should be increased towards acquisition cost. 
The Committee has further recommended that the allocation under present 
Sampoorna Gramin Rozgar Yojna scheme should be doubled and the expansion 
of the Antyodaya Anna Yojana be initiated.

Statement 
Joint Statement issued on the occasion of 5th Session of 
 India-Russia Joint Working Group on Afghanistan—17-18 July 2002 
The fifth meeting of the India-Russia Joint Working Group on 
Afghanistan was held in New Delhi on 17-18 July, 2002. Foreign Secretary 
134 

[1 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Kanwal Sibal led the Indian delegation to the meeting. H.E. Mr. Vyacheslav 
I.Trubnikov, First Deputy Foreign Minister led the Russian delegation. 
They noted positively the developments in Afghanistan, the 
implementation of the Bonn Agreements, and convening of the Loya Jirga in 
June. They looked forward to the consolidation of political, security and 
reconstruction processes in Afghanistan so that peace and stability could be 
restored on a durable basis and roots of terrorism eradicated. 
They reiterated their determination to continue supporting the 
reconstruction effort and the political consolidation process. 
Concern was expressed at continuing activity of Taliban and Al-Qaida 
elements and recent killing of Afghan Vice President Haji Abdul Qadeer by 
the forces of instability and intolerance. They agreed that the regrouping of Al-
Qaida and Taliban cadres in Afghanistan, and on its southern and south-
eastern borders, presents a serious threat to Afghanistan and to regional peace 
and stability. 
The two sides welcomed and supported the key continuing coordinating 
role of the United Nations in post-conflict reconstruction and rehabilitation of 
Afghanistan, noted the UN contribution to mobilising international 
humanitarian aid and establishing the new administrative institutions in 
Afghanistan. 
In view of the need to further strengthen the universal international legal 
basis for combating terrorism a detailed exchange of views took place on the 
ways to expedite the conclusion of the work in the UN on the Indian draft 
Comprehensive Convention against International Terrorism and the Russian 
draft International Convention for the suppression of Acts of Nuclear 
Terrorism. The sides agreed to continue coordinating their efforts aimed at 
achieving this goal. 
The two sides reiterated that terrorism cannot be justified on any 
grounds and must be eradicated wherev er it exists. They recalled that UN 
Security Council Resolution 1373 reaffirmed the principle that every State has 
the duty to refrain from organizing, instigating, assisting or participating in 
terrorist acts in another State or acquiescing in organized activities within its 
territory directed towards the commission of such 
135 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2002] 
acts, and further mandated that all States must refrain from providing any 
form of support, active or passive, to entities or persons involved in terrorist 
acts. 
They stressed the need for Pakistan to fulfil its stated commitment to end 
cross-border terrorism and extremism, not allow infiltration through the line 
of control and to fulfil its obligation asumed for suppressing the activities of 
terrorist groups based in Pakistan controlled territories. 
The two sides also discussed the situation in Central Asia, 
Transcaucusus, and issues relating to emerging threats to regional and 
international peace and stability. 
The delegations stressed that the interaction of Russia and India in 
combating international terrorism constituted an important component of 
strategic partnership between the two countries. The Sides confirmed their 
firm intention to further strengthen their anti terrorism cooperation based on 
summit-level agreements. 
The two sides agreed that the next meeting of the Joint Working Group 
would be held in Moscow on mutually convenient dates.

passengers from Agartala to Kolkata through Bangladesh; and 
140 

[1 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA

and lengthy journey by road from Agartala to Kolkata via Assam? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH ): (a ) The Government of India has 
repeatedly proposed to the Government of Bangladesh to provide facilities for 
transit of goods and passengers to the north eastern States, including Tripura, The

withdraw MFN status to Pakistan in view of the latter's continued support to cross 
border terrorism against India;

141 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to (c) Government have taken 
appropriate diplomatic and other measures in view of Pakistan's continued support 
to cross border terrorism against India.These included the decision to recall the 
Indian High Commissioner from Islamabad; terminate the services of 
Samjhauta Express and the Delhi-Lahore bus service with effect from 1 st 
January, 2002; reduce the strength of the respective High Commissions in the two

Pakistan a list of 20 fugitives from law with the request that they be 
apprehended and handed over to India.

monitors the situation and taken necessary and appropriate action.

Assistance to Afghanistan 
1695. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of all types of aid and assistance given to Afghanistan for its 
reconstruction; 
(b) the terms and conditions of such an assistance; 
(c) whether India is involved in any manner in Afghanistan's political 
process and its reconstruction; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to (d) India is committed to 
providing and has provided extensive humanitarian, project and financial 
assistance to Afghanistan. Government has announced a financial commitment 
of US$ 100 million for reconstruction and rehabilitation projects in Afghanistan. Out 
of this, on 10th July, 2002, the government transferred a sum of US$ 10 million 
into the account of Afghan government as budget subsidy. In addition, during the 
visit of H.E. Mr Hamid Karzai, Chairman of then Afghan Interim Administration 
to India in February this year, Prime Minister had announced an assistance of US$ 
10 million for various project related assistance to Afghanistan. Some of the 
major projects that have been implemented include supply of medical stores and 
medical services; artificial limbs center in Kabul; gifting of 50 buses to the Afghan 
government; training of Afghan diplomats at the Foreign Service Institute in New 
Delhi; deputation of English Language teachers to Afghanistan; computerization of 
Afghan Foreign Ministry; setting up of computer training center in Kabul, and 
training of Afghan Police Officers and cadets in India. Projects under 
consideration include in the fields of Water and Power, Agriculture, Education, 
Information and Broadcasting and Road Construction. 
Government is also in the process of finalizing details for handing over 
of three aircraft from Air India to Ariana Afghan Airlines.

[1 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA

food aid.The operationalization of this commitment faced some transit related 
difficulties. Government is now discussing with the World Food Programme 
options to operationalize part of this commitment in alternative forms, such as 
high protein biscuits for school feeding programme. 
Government has also been associated with various international efforts 
aimed at promoting reconstruction, reconsiliation and stability in 
Afghanistan, including the Tokyo meeting, G-21 meetings, Afghan Support 
Group meetings, Bonn Process, Emergency Loya Jirga and meetings held in 
Geneva to discuss rebuilding of Afghan security structures.

Enactment of Emigration of Amendment Bill, 2002 
1705. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MU RTHY: Will the Minister of 
LABOUR be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to enact the Emigration Amendment 
Bill, 2002 to facilitate setting up a Central Manpower Ex port Promotion 
Council and to constitute the Indian Overseas Welfare Fund; 
(b) whether this proposed enactment would sort out the problems being 
faced by the lowpaid emigrants to  Gulf countrie s like Ayahs and 
housemaids; and 
(c) whether there were proposals from the Overseas recruitment/ travel 
agents registered with his Ministry to take care of social welfare/ insurance 
requirements for housemaids and if so, whether Government would enlist 
their participation by making suitable provisions in the proposed Bill? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR 
(SHRI ASHOK PRADHAN): (a) to (c) The Government propose to enact the 
emigration (Amendment) Bill, 2002 to set up the Central Manpower Export 
Promotion Council and constitute Indian  Overseas Workers' Welfare Fund. 
The functions of the Council will be promotion of employment opportunities 
for emigrants; projection of manpower services; collection of statistics and 
information relating to employment opportunities and matters connected 
therewith; collection and maintenance of statistics and information in respect 
of persons seeking employment; liaison with other export promotion 
agencies; recommendation to the Centra l Government about the standards 
and guidelines for overseas employment; and administration of Indian 
Overseas Workers' Welfare Fund. The proposed Indian Overseas Workers' 
Welfare Fund will meet the contingencies, such as making the payment to the 
Embassies or High Commissions for arranging return ticket for the workers 
who get stranded in the foreign countries; meeting the cost of transportation 
of dead bodies of the workers, grantin g financial assistance to such workers 
who become partially or permanently disabled and providing relief for such 
other causes as may be specified in  the rules.The assistance would not, 
however, be provided to illegal migrants. 
Two persons representing the Recru iting Agents will be Members of 
the proposed Council.

Wage disparity 
1709. SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state:. 
(a) whether it is a fact that women are not paid wages equal to their men 
counterparts in agricultural sectors in most of the States; and 
(b) if so, the steps being taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR 
(SHRI ASHOK PRADHAN): (a) and (b) Women Workers in agricultural 
sector come under the unorganized sector and their wages are paid as per 
provisions of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. The Act does not make any 
distinction on the basis of sex.

1711. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Win the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is a recent Supr eme Court Judgment regarding 
imposition of strict punishment on employer for engaging child labour; 
(b) if so, the details of the directions as issued by the Supreme Court; 
(c) whether Government have issued any mandatory orders to all the 
States to implement and monitor the Supreme Court's directions in this regard; 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(e) whether Government have introducted any scheme to eradicate child

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR 
(SHRI ASHOK PRADHAN): (a) and (b) The Hon'ble Supeme Court in its 
judgment dated 10th December, 1996 in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 465/1986, has 
given certain directions regarding the manner in which the children working in 
the hazardous occupations are to be withdrawn from work and rehabilitated. 
These include payment of compensation amounting to Rs. 20,000/- by the 
offending employer for every child employed in contravention of the 
provisions of the Act. 
(c) Government has issued detailed guidelines to all State/UT 
Governments for implementation of the directions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court. 
(d) Does not arise. 
(e) to (g) The Government of India has been implementing two 
schemes for the benefit of children withdrawn from work namely the Scheme 
of National Child Labour Projects (NCLPs) and the Scheme of Grants-in-aid to 
Voluntary Organisations.The major activity under the NCLP is the running of 
special schools/centres largely through Non-Government Organisations, for 
rehabilitation of children withdrawn from work through non-formal education, 
vocational tranining, nutrition, health care, stipend etc. At present 100 NCLPs 
are under implementation in 13 child labour endemic states for the coverage of 
2.11 lakh working children. Under the Scheme of Grants-in-aid, Non-
Government Organisations are assisted directly for taking up projects for the 
rehabilitation of child labour.

Cess Act, 1996 and the Beedi and Cigar Workers (Conditions of 
Employment) Act, 1966 which are also applicable to certain categories of

providing social security to other sp ecified unorganized sector workers are 
the Beedi Workers' Welfare Fund Act, 1976; the Iron Or e, Manganese Ore 
and Chrome Ore Mines Labour Welfare Fund Act, 1976 and the Cine

ILO Convention 
1715. SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA: 
SHRI BALWANT SINGH RAMOOWALIA: 
Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India attended the plenary session of the ILO held in 
Geneva in the month of June, 2002; 
(b) if so, whether Government have made their stand clear and 
emphasized that Child labour is closely linked to poverty and illiteracy which 
are being addressed with urgency; 
(c) if so, what are the st eps Government have taken to eliminate child 
labour; 
172 

[1 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) the decisions taken in the ILO convention in this regard; and 
(e) to what extent Government have assured that child labour would be 
eliminated in India within a stipulated time? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR 
(SHRI ASHOK PRADHAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (e) India strongly endorsed the need to eliminate unconditionally 
the worst forms of child labour. It was mentioned that, the Government's 
strategy of attempting to eliminate this problem is through a sequential 
process begining with the worst formas and moving progressively towards 
hazardous & less hazardous forms of ch ild labour. It was also emphasized 
that, the problem of child labour is closely interlinked with poverty and 
illiteracy and the Government is addressing both these issues with urgency. 
The Government of India has been implementing two schemes for the 
benefit of children withdrawn from work namely the Scheme of National 
Child Lbaour Projects (NCLPs) and the Scheme of Grants-in-aid to 
Voluntary Organisations. At present 100 NCLPs are under implementation in 
13 child labour endemic states for the coverage of 2.11 lakh working 
children. In the Ninth Plan period the total allocation of funds for child 
labour Schemes was Rs. 249.60 crore. A proposal for an enhanced allocation 
for the Tenth Plan has been made. 
Government is committed to the goal of eradication of child labour in 
all its forms. Considering the nature and magnitude of the problem, a 
gradual, sequential approach has been adopted to withdraw and rehabilitate 
child labour beginning with children working in hazardous occupations.

1736.    SHRI SUDARSHAN AKARAPU:   
SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA:

(b) The Approach Paper to the Tenth Five Year Plan as approved by the 
National Development Council has proposed that the Tenth Plan should aim 
at an indicative target of 8 per cent GDP growth for the period 2002—07. 
It also states that: 
Economic growth cannot be the only objective for national planning 
and indeed over the years, development objectives are being defined not just 
in terms of increases in GDP or per capita income but broader in terms of 
enhancement of human well being. This includes not only an adequate level

basic social services especially education, health, availability of drinking 
water and basic sanitation. It also includes the

groups, reduction in disparities, and greater participation in decisionmaking.

percentage points by 2012; 
(ii)  Providing gainful high-quality employment to the addition to the 
labour force over the Tenth Plan period; 
(iii) All children in school by 2003; a ll children to complete 5 years of 
schooling by 2007; 
(iv) Reduction of gender gaps in literacy and wage rates by at least 50% 
by 2007; 
(v)  Reduction in the decadal rate  of population growth between 2001 
and 2011 to 16.2%; 
(vi)  Increase in Literacy rate to 75% within the Plan period; 
(vii)  Reduction of infant mortality rate (IMR) to 45 per 1000 live births 
by 2007 and to 28 by 2012; 
(viii)  Reduction of maternal mortality ratio (MMR) to 2 per 1000 live 
births by 2007 and to 1 by 2012; 
(ix)  Increase in forest and tree cover to 25% by 2007 and 33% by 2012; 
(x)  All villages to have sustained access to potable drinking water within 
the Plan period; 
(xi)  Cleaning of major polluted rivers by 2007 and other notified 
stretches by 2012. 
The Tenth Plan is under formulation.

1738.   SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN: 
SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) the criteria laid down for giving special category status to the States; 
(b) the States, which have been given the special category status, the 
minimum period of special category status any state can enjoy;

(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) The Special Category Status is 
given to those States which are having a strategic location on the border with 
neighbouring countries, hilly terrain, inadequate economic and social 
infrastructure, predominantly large tr ibal population, limited and weak 
resource base compared to development needs.

Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim.Tripuraand Uttaranchal. The 
issue relating to the inclusion and/or exclusion of a State for the Status of 
Special Category has to be decided by the National Development Council (NDC). 
(c) Since the State of Karnataka does not have all these features, it 
is not included under Special Categor y State. Moreover, devastation by 
drought or other natural calamities is not a criterion for eligibility to be a 
Special Category State. However, the 49th meeting of the NDC decided

Special Category Status to States should be examined.

meeting taken by the Union Agriculture Minister with Agriculture and Relief

212

1756. DR. VIJAY MALLYA: W ill the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the number of Small Scale 
Industries closed down in Karnatak a due to various reasons like power 
hike, costly labour, etc; 
(b) if so, whether Government have provided any incentives to these units 
to revive and strengthen their performance; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE ): (a) The information on 
closed units is not maintained centrally. However, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) 
compiles data on sick SSI units financed by scheduled commercial Banks. As per 
the latest information available with the RBI, there were 4400 sick units in the State 
of Karnataka by the end of March, 2001. 
(b) and (c) The Government is fully seized of the incidence of industrial 
sickness among SSI units and has taken various measures to facilitate timely 
identification and rehabilitation of potentially viable sick units, which inter-alia 
include institutional mechanism in the form of State-level Inter-Institutional 
Committees (SLIICs), Special Rehabilitation Cells in Banks and State Financial 
Institutions and elaborate guidelines issued by the RBI for extending 
rehabilitation assistance to eligible units. 
Further, for rehabilitation of sick/closed units, Government of 
Karnataka has also been providing assistance in the form of Seed Margin Money 
at 25% of the project cost subject to a maximum of Rs. 2.50 lakhs, waiver of 
fixed charges during closure period, payment of arrears of energy bill in 
instalments and waiver of interest for closure period.

CALLING ATTENTION TO MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE 
Issues arising out of decision of VSNL Board to invest Rs. 1200 crores in  
Tata Tele Services Ltd. 
SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Madam, I beg to call 
the attention of the Minister of. Co mmunications and Information Technology 
on the issues arising out of the decision of the VSNL Board to invest Rs. 1200 
crores in TATA Tele Services Ltd. 
[The Vice-Chairman, Shri Suresh Pachouri, in the Chair.] 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN): Sir, the Government has 
disinvested 25 per cent Government equi ty in Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd. to a 
strategic partner, M/s. Panatone Finves t Limited through due disinvestment 
process. The Share Purchase Agreement (SPA) was signed on 6 th February, 
2002 and the Share Holder Agreement (SHA) was signed on 13 th February 
2002. The strategic partner paid the consideration on 13 th February, 2002 and 
took over the management control of VSNL. 
A notice for convening the 127 th meeting of the Boar d of Directors of 
VSNL for 28 th May, 2002 was received on 21 st May, 2002. Agenda for the 
meeting included an agenda item B.11 "to consider inter-corporate investment 
up to Rs. 1200 crore in the equity of an Indian company holding Basic Service 
Operator (BSO) license." No details about the targeted company were given in 
the agenda item. 
The Board meeting was attended by  one of the two Government 
nominee Directors, namely Shri Rakesh Kumar, Sr. DDG (SU), Department of 
Telecommunications- Shri Y.S. Bhave,  Joint Secretary, Department of 
Information and Technology, the other Government nominee Director could 
not attend the meeting as he was on tour abroad. 
The Government Director, Shri Ra kesh Kumar, has informed that 
during the meeting, a presentation wa s made by Director (Operations) of 
VSNL, giving justification for the need for making such an inter-corporate 
investment without mentioning the targeted company. The Government 
230 

[1 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Director has further informed DoT that during the meeting, he made several 
observations and raised objections on the above matter. 
Immediately after the Board m eeting, VSNL informed the Stock 
Exchange that the Board of Directors  of VSNL had approved the inter-
corporate investment of up to Rs. 1200 crores in the equity share capital of 
Tata Tele Services Ltd. A committee of three Directors, vik. Shri Subodh 
Bhargava, Shri S.K.Gupta and Shri N. Srinath was constituted to undertake all 
such acts and deeds in relation to such inter-corporate investment. 
On 29 th May, 2002, the Government nominee Director through a 
letter addressed to VSNL disputed the fa ct that it was a unanimous decision 
as he had raised objections during the me eting. Further he did not give any 
positive consent to the proposal. He also raised certain other issues regarding 
late receipt of notice and incomplete agenda material. 
However, VSNL through a letter of 30m May, 2002, refuted the above 
position mentioned by the Government nominee Director. The Government 
nominee Director in rebuttal reiterated his stated position through his letter 
dated 31sl May, 2002 that the decision was not unanimous. 
On 31s' May, 2002, the Department of Telecom, wrote toVSNL that 
without prejudice to the stand of the Government Director and notwithstanding 
what transpired and happened so far, the scope and the terms of reference of 
the Committee appointed by VSNL Board may be again set out and redefined 
to include full analysis and consideration of the desirability of such an 
investment by VSNL in Tata Tele Servic es Limited and, thereafter, the matter 
may be taken to the Board for a final decision. It was also suggested that one 
of the Government Directors may be made a member of the said Committee. 
After further exchange of correspondence, VSNL accepted the 
suggestions of the Department of Teleco m and on the issue of the investment 
in Tata Tele Services Ltd., VSNL Board has constituted a Committee in 
consultation with the Government, which includes a Government nominee 
Director, Shri Y.S. Bhave, together with Shri Subodh Bhargava, Shri S. K. 
Gupta and Shri N. Srinath. The sc ope and terms of reference of the 
Committee are as follows: 
a) to study and decide the quantum and the valuation/price at which the 
investment will be made by VSNL in TTSL at various points of time; 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2002] 
b) to decide the trenches and periodicity of investment in TTSL; 
c) to negotiate, finalise and execute shareholders' agreements and 
other contractual arrangements with TTSL to best protect the 
interests of VSNL in respect of the investment; 
d) to determine conditions of draw down of the investment to TTSL 
linked to defined milestones to be achieved by TTSL; 
e) to play a constructive role in the manner in which TTSL utilizes and 
applies the investment; 
f) to identify and quantify any additi onal investment opportunities which 
are more attractive and submit the same to the Board for its 
consideration; 
g) such other functions may be delegated to it by the Board from time to 
time. 
The Committee is expected to submit its report by 15th August, 2002. 
The first meeting of the Committee was held on 29 th July.    The next 
meeting will be on 8m August, 2002. 
Further, the Department of Telecom (DoT) has been informed by the 
Government Director that during the 128th Board Meeting of VSNL held on 29th 
July, 2002, the VSNL Board has agreed to take on record various letters from 
Government Director (dated May 29, May 31 and July 25, 2002) indicating his 
objections/observations and reservations  on the proposal of VSNL for inter-
corporate investment up to the level of  Rs. 1200 crores in the equity of an 
Indian  company holding BSO licence. 
Through active participation by the nominated Government Director 
in the Committee and both the Government Directors on the Board, 
Government will make all efforts to protect its 26 per cent equity interest in the 
Company.

Now, what has been the consequence? Not only is there a negative figure, but 
the overall debt liabilities of the States, which were just Rs.53,660 crores in

devolution from the Centre to a particu lar State -- I would not like to mention

the Central Plan assistance -- and t he State's interest payment was Rs. 1408 
crores. In other words, the entire share of Central taxes was completely eaten 
up to pay the interest payment for t he year concerned; further, an additional 
amount of Rs. 3 crores had to be given from the Exchequer. Therefore, where 
is the money for development? How did it nappen? The other day, the Leader 
of the House and the hon. Finance Minist er very correctly pointed out that he

of a State Government, who has had a ve ry long innings, has identified four 
critical issues because of which the Stat es have come to this state. One is, of 
course, the implication of the Fifth Pay Commission; and, here, most 
respectfully, I must submit to the h on. Finance Minister and the Union; - 
because, once upon a time, I had the privilege of occupying that office -- 
whether we can afford to be populist. This is a plain question which is staring 
at our face. I remember, I had also set up a Pay Commission. I think the Third 
Pay Commission was set up during my time. And my colleagues sitting on my 
left are still criticising me for the decisions I took both on the Pay Commission 
and on

looked  at  article  292  or  293,   which  was   inserted   in  the

Sir, it is a well-known and accepted fact that the State Governments are 
passing through an economic crisis. I would like to sum up the economic 
position of the States as pe r the Report of the Reserve Bank of India. Sir, the 
fiscal position of the State Governments has been under stress since mid-80's.    
I am quoting the Reserve Bank of India Report: "While the gross

resulted from the revenue deficit and t he States' fiscal stress stems from the 
inadequacy of receipts in meeting t he growing expenditure. The level of 
resource flows to the States is determin ed by the efforts of the States in the 
generation of their own resources as well as resources transferred from the 
Centre. And the declining tax and non-tax GDP ratios have adversely affected

made to the people of the States, the State Governments have been promising

not expressing the views of a particular party. They are trying to stretch

impossible situation. The revenue account was in a huge deficit and even 
future revenues had already been drawn and spent completely. Besides this, 
a huge mountain of public debt and unpaid liabilities was transferred to us as 
a legacy. 
Now our Chief Minister has launched a bold programme of fiscal 
reforms, covering all major issues, namely, public transport, public distribution 
of rice, power sector, expenditure reforms , tax reforms, restructuring of public 
sector undertakings, disinvestment, good governance, etc. The Government of 
Tamil Nadu has held joint discussions with the Ministry of Finance, 
Government of India, on a medium-term fiscal reform programme, for which a 
memorandum of understanding will be signed shortly. Thus, on our part, we 
have undertaken comprehensive reforms necessary for restoring the fiscal 
health of Tamil Nadu. This will take time to bear good results. 
288 

[1 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
The fiscal problems that we face are very complex and literally 
insurmountable. As you are aware, the States have very limited potential for 
raising resources. Tamil Nadu is one of the highest taxed States in the county 
as can be seen from the States Own Re venues - NSDP ratio. We have been 
hit by problems ignored by the previous Government, drastic fall in our share 
of Central taxes and reduced tax collections due to the recessionary trends in 
the economy, a combination of factors which make it impossible for us to 
handle the crisis on our own. The current fiscal crisis has been thrust on us 
and we are doing our best to retrieve the situation. We can be successful if the 
Government of India appreciates our efforts and lends us a helping hand. The 
former Finance Minister, Mr. Yashwant Sinha, had constituted a Committee of 
State Finance Ministers to examine and recommend measures to address the 
fiscal problems afflicting the States in a meeting on June 12, 2002. The fiscal 
crisis has already been with us for a while and the situation has now become 
untenable. It is a national crisis. Some immediate corrective steps have to be 
taken pending receipt of the report of the Committee of State Finance 
Ministers. I suggest the Union Government may consider the following 
suggestions immediately to bring some re lief to the State Governments, (a) In 
response to our hon. Chief Minister's request, a grant package of Rs.3000 
crores should immediately be conceded to Tamil Nadu so as to bring in some 
liquidity into the State's fiscal system, (b) The normal ways and means 
advance allowed by the Reserve Bank of India may be enhanced by 50 per 
cent of the existing limit for all States t ill such time the report of the Committee 
of State Finance Ministers is implemented, (c) There should be an immediate 
moratorium on annuities payable by the State Governments to the 
Government of India pending consideration and extending relief on the issue 
of debt burden of the States, (d) A debt relief package to enable State 
Governments to substitute their high cost  debt with the Government of India 
should immediately be worked out. This should afford substantial relief and 
not merely tinker with the problem. 
The States like Tamil Nadu have taken bold initiatives for reforms 
and it is now for the Government of I ndia to respond in full measure. I hope 
that the Finance Minister will agree to my suggestions pending receipt of the 
full report of the Committee of State Finance Ministers and extend an early 
relief package to all the State Governments. 
Now Tamil Nadu is reeling under severe drought.    Most of the 
districts are in the grip of drought.   In villages, there is no drinking water.   In

officers of the Ministry of Finance, an d it would be resolved within a week's 
time. (Interruptions) 
I don't want to take the time of the House by reanalysing what almost 
every Member has analysed, as to what is the state of finances and what we 
have done. As I said just last evening,  in the other House, I am adult enough 
to know the realities of life.  I, therefore, accept that t he world is not as it ought 
to be; the world is as it. is; and I have inherited the world 
310 

[1 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
as it is. Therefore, I have to work, in th at world, not in an ideal world. In that 
situation, Madam, I believe, I need not go into the background of the 
profligacy of approach on the recommendations of the Pay Commission and 
the consequence of it on the finances, not just of the Union Government, but, 
indeed, of every State Government. It is true that there ar e 3tates who are, 
today, spending almost 80% of what go es by the name of Plan allocation, if 
not more, just on meeting the revenue expenditure of the State, on salary. 
Pranab Babu read out that passage from the Planning Commission 
document, it is not a passage that delig hts anybody. It is not a passage with 
an expression of exaltation. It is a passage of realism, which, I believe, for the 
first time, has pointed out that this is what is happening. We have, all of us, 
without exception, brought about this situation, because of competitive and 
unchecked populism. I think there was a phrase used here, 'you have brought 
too much politics in economics and too little economic thought into political 
conduct.' It needs to be reversed. Can it be done overnight? No, I don't think 
so. I am very glad that this discussion has taken place. It was a discussion of 
very high importance. If the States' financ es we are able to cure, we will be 
taking a major joint step towards this. Without any monitoring, we are all guilty 
of profligate expenditure in the grace of declining revenues. I am not going into 
the declining revenues or what percentages  of the GDP. I am really sitting in 
front here now up to very experienced economists. So, I say this as a non-
economist, with a great degree of repetit ion, I do not think fault can be found 
with the formulation of tax policy. A sufficient thought has gone into policy 
formulation, policy thin king and in taxation matters that I think has reached a 
point where there is very little that c an be put there by way of improvement in 
terms of thought of polic y. What has not kept pace is really the tax 
administration. If we are to address ours elves to tax administration, whether it 
is tax administration here at the Central level or whether it is at the State level, 
I do believe that we will be addressing and we will be putting our finger on the 
crux of the problem. I again say this with a great degree of trepidation , as a 
non-economist - but I am addressing it in  that form and I felt considerable 
rewarded and satisfied when the long serpentine queues for the Permanent 
Account Numbers or settlements or filing claims or returns, etc., required the 
Ministry of Finance to extend the last date of filing returns by nine days. That 
to my mind, is not a negative but it is  some movement forward. But at the 
present moment, is tax satisfac tory to the ratio of the GDP?     No, it is not.    
We must improve it.    Let us try 
311 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2 002] 
improving the tax administration in its totality. When I say the tax 
administration I am really referring to all aspects, all shortcomings of the tax 
administration. We have limited resource s on account of which is an area of 
concern to me is very declining capital investment. Asset creation is a 
consequence of capital investment. We are particularly in States witnessing an 
absence of investment. An absence of investment is really mortgaging the 
future. When I look at the profile of inve stment in the States, when I see that 
there is now emerging in our federation a disproportion of investment -- some 
of it is inevitable between coastal I ndia and hinterland India. And it is 
proportion of investment, capital formatio n, this is an area that we are seized 
of because some States are receiving and are paying a much greater attention 
than other States are. I do not wish to go into the listing of the States. But 
there has to be a greater awareness in the State itself of not to be left behind 
in this process and enter into this rather a competitive environment. Madam, 
we have to staunch this haemorrhage and see what our priorities are. I am not 
approaching this issue with any ideological baggage. I am approaching this 
issue as a practical problem and to be attempted to be resolved with as much 
consensus on practical economic fiscal steps, and not attempting to arrive at 
an ideological unity which is impossible. So, let us try and work out, at least, 
some practical steps for a consensus so t hat we can say, 'We ll, these four or 
five steps we could take.' 
The fundamentals have to be approach ed. And, therefore - I borrow, 
again, this very flattering phrase of Pranabbabu's -- as a federal Finance 
Minister, I had my first interaction wi th the Committee of Finance Ministers. 
There are two Committees. The first one is  addressing itself to the important 
aspect of Value Added Tax. Pranabbabu  talked about the Consignment Tax. 
Unless we have the VAT, the whole issue, of services being drawn unto it, 
equalisation of tax regime, what to do in place of Octroi, which is really 
Consignment Tax, will not be resolv ed. Some States have apprehensions; 'In 
switching over from what is today to VAT tomorrow, are we likely to lose 
something, and if we lose something, who will then stand up for us and 
compensate us?' I think, the Central Government has to stand up, with the 
States, sit with the Central Ministers. So, we instituted the Committee, which is 
only of the Finance Ministers. I am informed by them that they had done about 
98 per cent of their work. I am not pushing them. I am glad that they have 
arrived a consensuous bag of solutions, themselves. I am not pushing them, 
on time. I am waiting for them   to   comp lete   their job. We   were   earlier 
scheduled   to   meet 
312 

[1 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
tomorrow, the 2 August, 2002. Because of certain Parliamentary pressures, I 
have requested for the postponement of this  by just one week, to meet on the 
9lh August. There is a second Committee. And I am flattered that the Finance 
Ministers of the States asked me to  Chair the second Committee. We have 
agreed on the composition of it. I hav e no difficulty if the State Finance 
Ministers wish to have more Finance Ministers in it. What are we addressing in 
this? We will address questions like how to mitigate the pressure of the 
recommendations of the last Pay Commission's Report. We have some ideas 
which we have already thought about. In this Committee of State Finance 
Ministers, once we arrive at some  consensus, we have intentions of 
recommending to the hon. Prime Minister to call a meeting of Chief Ministers 
of all the States so that whatever we  are able to recommend is then approved 
by the Chief Ministers. We  wish to approach this as an exercise in which 
everyone has a say, everyone is a partner, and everyone is committed to 
achieving those objectives, without one or  the other trying to play politics on 
the issue. So, one is about the Pay Commission. 
The other very important issue is about debt swapping. As the 
Finance Ministry, we have set that in moti on. I accept that. If the interest rates 
are softer, why should States be saddled with the highest interest rates? We 
have almost completed the exercise, in an orderly fashion; how to arrange for 
this debt swapping so that t he States are able to retire that high interest or 
high cost debts and are able to take up lower cost debts. This also, I hope, we 
will be able to finalise at the State Finance Ministers' meeting. 
The third that we hope to be able to finalise, in this very meeting -
because the Report of the other State Finance Minist ers' meeting would have 
come to us -- is the question of Value Added Tax. Fourthly, Shri Asim 
Dasgupta, the Finance Minister of West  Bangal had said that we need to 
approach this issue and the limitations that the Reserve Bank has placed on 
the access to finance that t he States have. We will approach it with a very 
practical approach in our mind. We do not have any intention to cause any 
inconvenience to any States. All citi zens of the Union of India are the 
responsibility of the Finance Ministry of India. There cannot be any distinction 
between one citizen and the other. Certainly not, on any caste, gender, 
religion, faith, which Stat e you belong to or what political persuasions you 
subscribe. You cannot have an econom y or the management of the Finance 
Ministry in a manner that a particular policy will

apply to a particular region or State. These are broadly the four issues that the

Statement 
(a\ to (f) The equipment has not been approved by Research Designs and 
Standard Organisation (RDSO). However, M/s. Mohata Overseas (Pvt. Ltd.) 
had approached RDSO for explaining the product which is claimed to enhance 
the life of batteries RDSO requested the firm to furnish the technical 
specifications, maintenance requirements, operating instructions, details fo 
performance feed back from the users etc. However, these details could not 
be submitted by the firm. In the meantim e, the firm in consultation with RDSO 
and Alambagh shops Lucknow demonstrated the equipmet by reviving two 
coach sets of rejected batteries in workshops.These revived batteries were 
subjected to life cycle tests and could survive only 6—8 cycles as against 
normal about 21 cycles for new batteries. These regenerated batteries were put 
on field trials by Northern Railway in two coaches. The trials remained 
inconclusive as the batteries had to be replaced in less than a year.The firm was 
again requested by RDSO furnish the technical details, maintenance 
requirement, operating instructions, deta ils-of such system supplied so far, 
details of performance feedback from t he users etc. Howeve r, these details 
are yet to be furnished by the firm. The firm subsequently made a presentation 
in Railway Board on 31.7.2002 wherein they were again requested to provide 
the technical details from Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM), the names 
of the customers to whom the equip ment was supplied and the performance 
certificate from the users so as to establish reasonably the claim made by 
them. Based on the details to be furnished by the firm, the issue will be 
examined by RDSO before taking a final decision in the matter.

Statement 
(a) to (c) A National River Conservation Authority exists under the 
Chairmanship of Prime Minister to fana lize the policy frame-work and oversee 
the implementation of conservation and management plans of rivers and lakes. 
A water Quality Assessment Authority has been constituted under the 
provisions of Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 in May 2001 with Secretary of 
the Ministry of Environment and Forests as Chairman, for water quality 
management of surface and ground water bodies. A National River Conservation 
Plan is under implementation for conservation and pollution abatement of 
polluted rivers. Under this Plan, conservation and pollution abatement works 
have been approved in 153 towns along the polluted stretches of 28 rivers in 17 
States. The estimated cost of these works is Rs. 3343 crore against which 
Central grants amounting to Rs. 1068 crore have been released so far. 
Conservation and management of rivers is one of the monitorable targets under 
the Tenth Plan. For conservation and management of lakes, National Lake 
Conservation Plan is under implementation. Under this scheme, plans for 
conservation and management of 7 urban polluted lakes have been approved 
at an estimated cost of Rs. 27.22 crore. These projects are under 
implementation and Central grants amounting to Rs. 9.79 crore have been 
released to the State Governments concerned so far.

Sariska Tiger Reserve from 1.2.2002 to  date. Important reasons of death 
include infighting injuries, traumma, liver disease, poaching; and road 
accidents. The exact reason of death in case of two animals could not be

include:

(iii)   Regular patrolling by field staff and equipping them appropriately. 
(iv)   Improvement of the wildlife habitat and augmenting the water supply 
through water holes and anicuts. 
(v)   Involvement of local communities and Non-Governmental 
Organization in wildlife conservation efforts. 
(vi)   Strengthening of communication network. 
(d) Question does not arise.

categories of products. However, this mismatch is temporary and Government is 
making efforts to see that the demand is strengthened. Steps taken by the 
Government to raise consumption level of steel in the country, include (i) 
constitution of a National Campaign Committee to promote steel consumption 
through development of markets especially in the rural areas, (ii) encouraging 
usage of steel in new applic ation areas such as grain storage systems, crash 
barriers in highways and express ways, (iii) providing financial support to R&D

*295. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that foodgrains production in 2001-2002 had been 
estimated at 211.32 MT, according to the latest estimates; 
(b) whether this spells a growth rate of 7.8 per cent over last year's output 
and would impact favourably the GDP and food security; and 
(c) if so, what steps Government have taken to ensure that the growth and 
development of infrastructure for storage and distribution is adequate, to 
prevent crores of rupees worth of grain wastage? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH) : (a) and (b) Yes, 
Sir. 
(c) The Food Corporation of India (FCI ) is the main agency which provides 
the capacity for storage of foodgrains. Besides, constructing its own godowns, 
FCI also hire storage capacity from other sources such as the Central 
Warehousing Corporations (CWC), State Warehousing Corporations (SWCs), 
State Governments and Private Partie s. The storage capacity of CWC and 
SWCs is also utilised for storing other notified commodities like fertilisers, seeds, 
etc. the total storage capacity available with FCI, CWC, SWCs and State 
agencies procuring on behalf of FCI or having decentralized procurement is of 
the order of 87 million tonnes. 
With a view of augment existing storage facilities and to introduce bulk 
handling, storage and transportation of foodgrains in the country, the 
Government have announced a National Policy on handling, storage and 
transportation of foodgrains. According to the National storage policy, 
integrated bulk handling, storage and tr ansportation facilities for a total 
capacity of 21 lakh tonnes for wheat are proposed to be created in producing 
and consuming areas through Private Sector participation on Build-Own-
Operate (BOO) basis. The Government have also recently launched Gramin 
Bhandaran Yojana, under a Central Sector Scheme on Construction of Rural 
Godowns. The scheme envisages new storage c apacity of 18.50 lakh tonnes 
and modernisation of cooperative godowns of capacity 1.50 lakh tonnes.

RAJYA SABHA [2 A ugust, 2002] 
Decline in growth of soyabean in M.P. 
*298. SHRI KAILASH JOSHI: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) what are the reasons for decline in growth of soyabean in Madhya 
Pradesh; 
(b) whether ICAR has taken up any study in this regard in general, and worm 
affected crop in particular; 
(c) if not, what are the reasons therefor; and 
(d) whether Government propose to study the matter in depth; if so, by when? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) Soyabean is 
relatively new crop to India. In 1985 the areas of soyabean was about 1.34 mha 
which increased to 6.3 mha in 1998. Madhya Pradesh is the leading State of 
India for soyabean cultivation covering about 4.5 mha annually. In the initial 
years the growth rate of area, pro duction and productivity was very high. 
However, the area of soyabean in Madhya Pr adesh is under the process of 
stabilization which ranged between 4.46 mha in 1997 to 4.47 mha in the year 
2000-01. The productivity which was 764kg/ha in 1985 has reached 1100 kg/ha in 
1999-2000 wl lich is a positive growth. However, there has been decline in 
production in the last two years becaus e of unfavourable growing conditions in 
the State of Madhya Pradesh. 
(b) Yes Sir, the National Research Centre on Soyabean, Indore and All India 
Coordinated Research Project on Soyabean under ICAR have taken up studies to 
find out the reasons for low productivity of soyabean in general and worm 
affected areas in particular. Since soyabean is grown as rainfed kharif crop, 
adverse weather conditions affect the cr op drastically. Among the major factors 
responsible for low productivity are tjon-availability of good quality seed, 
cultivation under rainfed conditions and slow adoption of improved production 
technologies. In certain areas the crop is also affected by endemic diseases like 
rust (Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra) and insect pests like tobacoo caterpillar 
(Rajasthan). However, ICAR has developed rust tolerant varieties and integrated 
pest management practices for the control of important pests of soyabean. 
(c) and (d) Question do not arise.

1775. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased 
to state: 
† Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi. 
52 

[2 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether the Ministry of Agriculture or any other agency has 
conducted a study in Punjab, which shows that the State is heading towards 
ecological disaster and may turn into desert; 
(b) if so, the salient features of the study report; and 
(c) the reasons for the fall in the water level in rural areas and the 
measures for correcting the ground water imbalance in the State? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) An ICAR Fact Finding Committee 
submitted its Report in June, 1998 entitled "Decline in Crop Productivity in 
Haryana and Punjab: Myth or Reality?" The Committee was constituted by 
Hon'ble Agriculture Minister, Government of India to assess agricultural 
productivity issues in Punjab and Haryana. 
(b)The report highlighted that duri ng the Green Revolution period in 
seventies, inadequate attention was paid towards future demands of inputs, 
particularly of energy, water, fertilizers and pesticides. The effort apparently was 
towards maximization rather than optimization of resource inputs. Significant 
changes in cropping pattern also took place in the region. Now growth rate in 
productivity of rice and wheat show clearly a decline in some of the districts of 
Punjab. The important recommendations of the report include the following: 
1. Agriculture in the State of Punjab needs to be diversified through 
inclusion of dairy, poultry, horticulture, vegetables and similar other 
enterprises. 
2. Micro-level planning at the district and block level should be 
carried out to identify more suitable land use patterns. 
3. Research to develop new varieties of rice and wheat with higher yield 
potential should be strengthened. 
4. Farmers may be given incentive for introducing pulse crops and 
green manures for long term agricultural sustainability. 
5. For controlling salinity and waterlogging the saline water from the 
region needs to be disposed off to a safe disposal site. 
6. Pricing policy, for fertilizers, water and energy should have the long-
term sustainability dimension. 
53 

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2002] 
(c) Rapid increase in the number of tubewells from 1.92 lakhs in 1970-71 
to 8.95 lakhs in 1996-97 has resulted in over-exploitation of ground water in 70 out 
of 118 blocks of the State leading to decline in ground water level. The 
imbalance in the use of ground wa ter can be ameliorated though pr oper 
distribution of available water resources in the State, appropriate" crop 
planning and timely sowing of rice crop, ground water recharge projects in the 
Kandiregion and other potential sites, harvesting of rain water in paddy fields and 
village tanks, efficient use of saline and poor quality water and rationalization of 
water and energy pricing.

Wheat and paddy production 
1785.SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH:  
DR. ABRAR AHMED: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether production of paddy and wheat in India recorded a decline in 
2000-2001, compared to 1999-2000; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) the remedial steps proposed to improve the yield; and 
(d) the production of wheat and rice during 2001 -2002? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The overall rainfall during monsoon 2000 was deficient by 8% and 
this deficiency was accentuated during the subsequent seasons./in the western 
part of India, especially Rajasthan, Gujarat and Madhya Pr adesh, large areas 
faced moisture stress. The States of Bihar and West Bengal also faced moisture 
stress at the time of sowing of paddy. The deficient rainfalls resulted in lower area 
coverage under paddy and wheat, leading to reduction in production. 
(c) In order to improve the producti on and productivity of agricultural 
commodities including paddy and wheat, the Government have launched various 
initiatives such as promotion of watershed development programmes, 
emphasis on developing and promoting new technologies, measures for 
increasing availability of agricultural credit, price policy, Market Information 
Network and National Agriculture Insurance Scheme etc. which have enabled the 
country to achieve an upward trend in foodgrain production and productivity over a 
long period of time. However, year to 
 
74 

[2 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
year fluctuation in foodgrain/agricultural production take place due to agro-climatic 
conditions. For the year 2001 -2002, the country is likely to achieve an all time 
record production of over 211.32 million tonnes. 
(d) As per the Fourth Advance Estimates on 27.6.2002, the production of wheat 
and rice during 2001 -2002 is expected to be 71.47 million tonnes and 91.61 
million tonnes respectively.

HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) The Registration Committee constituted

food crops in the country only after satisfying itself regarding data on chemistry,

an Expert Committee in 2001 under the Chairmanship of Dr. A. Achuthan. The 
Committee concluded as follows:—

The Committee also recommended the ban on aerial spraying of 
pesticides in all cashew plantations in Kasargod district of Kerala, pesticide holiday 
for five years in Peria Division of Plantation Corporation of Kerala and promotion of 
Integrated Pest Management. On the direction of National Human Rights 
Commission, a study has been conducted by the National Institute of 
Occupational Health (NIOH) of the Indian Council of Medical Research and 
higher prevalence of unusual diseases like mental retardation, congenital

villages of Kasargod district of North Kerala has b een reported in their first 
report.

Losses due  to Soil Erosion 
1834. SHRIMATI N.R DURGA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the country was suffering heavy losses due to massive soil 
erosion; and 
(b) if so, the measures proposed to  maintain a balance between nature 
and development, ensuring environment-friendly growth? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMEN T AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALLU): (a) and (b) Soil erosion takes place due to natural factors like 
unstable geological formations of mountains heavy rains, cloudburst and biotic 
factors like faulty land use practices, construction activities, inadequate tree 
cover etc. in the catchment areas of t he major river systems. It is a major 
problem on degraded hilly slopes and areas prone to floods. However, there is 
no alarming report that the country is suffering from an unusual and 
unprecedented situation of soil erosion. 
Checking soil erosion and denudation in  the catchment areas of rivers, 
lakes and reservoirs in the interest of soil and water conservation is one of the 
basic objectives of the National Forest  Policy, 1988. The measures taken to 
check soil erosion include forest protection activities and Joint Forest 
Management Programme, National Afforestation Programme for plantation on 
degraded forest land, watershed development and soil conservation works on 
agricultural land etc. 
Special legislative measures like the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 are 
also in place to maintain a balance between nature and development. This Act 
regulates diversion of forest lands for non-forestry purposes and also provides 
for compensatory afforestation on equivalent/more area of non-
forest/degraded forest land. 
All these measures help to maintain a balance between nature and 
development, ensuring environment-friendly growth.

1849. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the basic norms binding recognition of educational 
institutions as "Deemed Universities';

College, Surathkal, Karnataka as a "deemed University'; 
(c) whether the Karnataka Government has recommended a few 
educational institutions for grant of Deemed University status; and 
(d) if so, the Centre's response thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERM A]: (a) University 
Grants Commission has laid down the guidelines for considering proposal for 
declaring an institution as Deemed to be University under Section 3 of the UGC 
Act, 1956. These guidelines inter-alia provide that, an institution should 
generally be; 
(i) Engaged in teaching programmes and research in chosen fields of 
specialization which are innovative and very high academic standards 
at the Master's (or equivalent) and/or research levels. It should also 
have a greater interface with society through extra mural, extension and 
field action related programmes. 
(ii) Making in its ateas of specializ ation, distinct contribution to the 
objectives of the University educ ation system through innovative 
programmes and on being recognized a9 a university capable of further 
enriching the university system as well as strengthening teaching and 
research in the institution and particularly in its area of specialization. 
(iii) Competent to undertake application-oriented programmes in emerging 
areas which are relevant and useful to various development sectors 
and to the society in general. 
(iv) institutions should have the necessary viability and a management capable 
of contributing to the university ideals and traditions. 
130 

[2 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Ordinarily, institutions affiliated to universities and which are offering only 
conventional degree programmes leading  to BA/B.Com/B.Sc. or MA/ 
M.Com/M.Sc, will not be considered for grant of deemed to be university status. 
However, such institution which is al so offering innovath/e programmes, and 
which has adequate resources, might be considered for recognition as a 
university. Supplimentary assistance for Innovation may be considered by the 
UGC only in such exceptional cases. 
Institutions which are imparting routin e type of instruction to full-time 
students or offering training programmes for in-service personnel, unless of 
high quality, would, generally, not qualify for recognition. 
In selective cases, outstanding research institutions specializing in Social 
Sciences, Sciences and Technology can be considered for research degree and 
highly specialized programmes at the Master's level. 
In case the institution is offeri ng a degree/diploma, professional 
subject(s), the academic programme(s) should be recognized by the 
concerned statutory authority e.g. Alt fndia Council for Technical Education (AiCTE), 
Medical Council of India (MCI), Dental Council of India (DCI), Central Council of 
Homoeopathy (CCH), Indian Nursing Council (FNC) etc. before it applies for a 
deemed to be university status under Section 3 of the UGC Act. 
This shall, however, not apply to de-novo institutions in the emerging areas 
with the promise of excellence, not yet fulfilling the prescribed guidelines of the 
UGC whose case will be considered for a provisional status for a Deemed to 
be University. 
(b) Ministry of Human Resource Development has granted Deemed to be 
University status to National Institut e of Technology Karnataka, Surathkal 
(formerly known as Karnataka Regional Engineering College, Surathkal). 
Notification was issued on 26th June 2002.

1850. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: W ill the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURE DEVELOPMENT be  pleased to state: 
(a) the number of students who committed suicide after examination results 
in different States, including Madhya Pradesh, during the last two years; 
(b) whether the trend is on the increase; 
(c) if so, the factors responsible for this; and 
(d) the steps taken by Government to solve the 'problem? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) to (d) A few 
cases of suicides related to examinations were reported in the news papers 
after declaration of Board results this year. The statistics in this regard are not 
reported to this Ministry. However, the Board of Secondary Education, 
Madhya Pradesh, Bhopal has informed that no student is reportd to have 
committed suicide following the declaration of CBSE and other equivalent 
examination results this year and during the preceding two years. The cases 
relating to depression and suicides are linked to a number of factors including 
individual personality, fast changing social dynamics, home environment, inability 
of children to cope with the demands and expectations of family, peer pressure 
and a situation in which career opportunities are very limited in relation to 
mounting number of aspirants and examinations being a major determinant of 
career path. 
The Central Board of Secondary E ducation (CBSE) ha s already taken 
several steps to help the students to overcome their difficulties like: 
• Arranging for a stress free environment in schools 
• Deciding on Introduction of like skill education 
• Elimination of overall aggregation of marks to reduce unhelathy 
competition among students 
•  Introduction of comprehensive and continous school based 
evaluation 
132 

12 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
• Providing facility of compartment examination in two subjects in Class 
X and one subject in Class XII 
• Providing three chances of compartment examination for Class X and 
XII 
• Restructuring of questions in some of the important subjects such as 
Science and Mathematics. 
• Publication of sample question papers and making schemes to 
familiarize teachers and students about the nature of questions and 
question papers 
Similarly, the Council for the Indian School Certificate Examinations (CISCE) 
has introduced measures like flexibility in the choice of subjects at the Secondary 
level, internal assessment, continuous  involvement of schools/teachers in 
updating and revising the prescribed curriculum etc. to facilitate learning and 
reducing stress on students. 
The CBSE has also starte d telecounselling on vo luntary basis by the 
educationists, psychologists, psychiatrists and seasoned principals of the 
schools. It starts functioning before and during the examinations and also during 
declaration of results to mitigate and def use the sense of anxiety and stress 
among the students. For 2002 examinations, CBSE had started helpline from 
31 centres in and outside the country. 
Recognising the importance of counselling parents in the matter the CBSE 
has written to all CBSE affiliated schools for organising such c ounselling 
sessions. A copy of the circular dated 10.07.2002 issued by the CBSE to all its 
affiliated schools giving suggestions to reduce stress and anxiety of students has 
been sent by the Ministry of Human Resource Development to all 
States/Govts./State Boards of Secondary Education for their information and 
use.

which contains goals for children in the four priority areas, namely, promoting 
healthy lives, providing quality education, protecting against abuse, exploitation 
and violence and combating HIV/ AIDS. The Indian delegation played a pivotal 
role and helped to facilitate a consensus on the Document. The Declaration 
was adopted by all countries through consensus. The Document urges the 
developed countries to mobilize resources for meeting the target of 0.7% of 
their Gross National Product (GNP) fo r Official Development Assistance

1860. DR. AKHILESH DAS: 
             SHRIAIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): 
Will the Minister of HUMAN R ESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Non-formal Education Programme has 
remained largely on paper for over two decades ever since it was launched in 1979-
80; 
(b) if not, how far the targets fixed under Eighth and Ninth Five Year Plans 
have remained unfulfilled, State-wise, and for the country as a whole; and 
.(c) whether the Non-formal Educati on Centres too remained mostly on 
paper in different States; if so, the mechanism put in place to muster their 
functioning? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [Dr. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) to (c) The 
scheme of Non-Formal Education (NFE) launched in 1979-80 was implemented 
by State/UT Governments and Voluntary Agencies. The scheme was evaluated, 
and based on the recommendations of the evaluating Agencies, it was modified as 
Education Guarantee Scheme and Alternative and Innovative Education 
(EGS&AIE).The scheme of Non-Formal Education was discontinued w.e.f., 1.4.2001 
and in its place the modified scheme of EGS&AIE was made operational from the 
same date. 
As on 31.3.2001,2.43 lakh and 0.58 lakh NFE Centre were reported 
functioning under State and Voluntary Sectors respectively. As and when any 
complaint was received, it was got investigated by a Joint Evaluation Team 
comprising the Officers of this Ministry/State Government/NCERT/ SCERT and 
on adverse report, the project in question was cancelled.
